name: Northeastern Pomo
confidence_why: Buckley 2023, McLendon 1973 and Halpern 1984 (as quoted by Walker 2016) agree that Northeastern Pomo stress is unpredictable, falling on the first or second syllable of the word with no known conditioning rule, though all of them rest on the thin field records of an extinct language (Halpern's 1939-40 notes and McLendon's one month of fieldwork).

catalog_quote: Primary stress can be reconstructed on the second syllable of most words (McLendon 1973: 34). It falls on the initial syllable where the root is just one syllable in length; essentially, the stress does not move off the root of the word. It is likely that this pattern arose from a strictly morphological root-initial pattern; given the frequency of words containing an instrumental prefix (§5.1), this would most often correlate with the second syllable, and that generalization was extended to unprefixed roots of at least two syllables, such as *bihˈše ‘deer’ and *šiʔˈba ‘body’ (Moshinksy 1976; Buckley 2014). ... In Northeastern the stress has often moved to the first syllable, but in other cases remains on the second, as in ˈbehše versus šiʔˈba. The conditioning factors for this shift have not been determined.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (marked in Halpern's 1940 transcriptions) falls on the first or second syllable of the word: on the second syllable in some disyllabic roots and in prefix+root stems, as in the rest of Pomoan (root stress), but shifted to the first syllable in many other disyllabic roots; the same word is sometimes recorded with either placement, and no conditioning factor has been found. Halpern himself (1984: 40, quoted by Walker 2016) saw a frequent but optional penultimate tendency, with the accent never falling after the root in long verb forms. Walker 2016 calls the system 'somewhat problematic' and Buckley 2014 says the pattern 'at present remains uncertain'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated. Buckley 2014 (slide 46) notes that Halpern transcribes some long words with two accents (šímitílda 'did you hear?', ʃímitká:li) and asks whether such words carry stress on both the first and the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Free variation between first- and second-syllable stress in the same form (šúʔu-ka: ~ šuʔú-ka: 'coyote', málaʔ ~ maláʔ 'ashes'); apparent rightward shift under suffixation (má:ti 'day' vs ma:tí-min 'sunrise'; húʔba: 'tongue' vs huʔbá:-wi 'with the tongue'; Walker's lexicon: root lengthening moves stress to the second syllable before locative -wi) against stable root stress in other words (č'íjit-ka: 'bird', tuhúl 'north'); possible sentence-rhythm effects (šilíma 'sit down!' vs ʔáma šílima 'you sit down!'). Mithun 1999 and van der Hulst et al. 2010 summarise the language simply as 'stress falls on roots'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms and short sentences from Halpern's one-week 1940 fieldwork with a single speaker (Santiago McDaniel); no audio analysed (McLendon's 1958 recordings of Minnie Bill are unanalysed, per Walker 2016). Buckley suggests phrase rhythm may shift placement; the language has been extinct since c. 1961, so the record cannot be extended.
new_statements.identity_note: Northeastern Pomo = 'Salt Pomo' (native čʰéʔe: fóka:), Stonyford, Colusa County; Glottolog nort2967 (language level, no dialects). All stress data derive from Halpern's 1940 notes with one speaker (Santiago McDaniel) plus earlier unaccented transcriptions (Barrett 1908, Merriam, Kroeber 1923); the community wordlist saved here distinguishes 'Stonyford language' from 'Paka Fokka language' variants but carries no stress information. The language has had no fluent speakers since c. 1961.

new_statements.quote: ... daughter languages have the following prosodic systems. In Pse and Ps the position of stress is phonologically conditioned. In Pse, stress always occurs on the first syllable. In Ps, according to Halpern, stress always occurs on the penult (on the penult of clauses according to Oswalt [personal communication]) ... Pn, Pc, Pne, and Pe have a phonemic accent that occurs mostly on the first or second syllable of a word. It is primarily a pitch accent (tone) in Pn and stress in Pc, Pne, and Pe. In Pe its location is partially predictable morphologically: stress always occurs on the root in verbs. There is, however, no synchronic basis for identifying roots in most nouns ...

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Northeastern Pomo has an empty rule, and the existing statement (Buckley 2020 §3.6, which itself cites McLendon 1973: 34) is labelled 'unclear or contradictory' (proto stress on the root/second syllable; in Northeastern 'often moved to the first syllable, but in other cases remains on the second', conditioning undetermined). McLendon's own synchronic characterisation is compatible with that and sharper: Pne stress is phonemic (unpredictable) and confined mostly to the first or second syllable, and it is a stress accent, not the pitch accent of Northern Pomo. So it refines the catalog from 'unclear' to 'lexical stress within a two-syllable left-edge window'. Caveat: th…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Northeastern Pomo (McLendon's 'Pne') has a phonemic, i.e. contrastive, stress accent whose position is not phonologically conditioned; it falls mostly on the first or second syllable of the word (a two-syllable left-edge window). McLendon gives no synchronic conditioning for Pne (she gives one only for Eastern, where verb stress is on the root) and reconstructs Proto Pomo accent as falling on the root syllable (which is the second syllable of most prefixed words).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets available.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Pne beyond 'mostly' on the first or second syllable (implying occasional other positions). Abbreviations in the quote: Pn Northern, Pc Central, Pne Northeastern, Pe Eastern, Ps Southern, Pse Southeastern.
new_statements.identity_note: McLendon's 'Pne' is Northeastern Pomo (Salt Pomo, Stonyford), the same variety as Glottolog nort2967 (Northeastern Russian River Pomo, ISO pef). It must not be confused with Northern Pomo ('Pn', nort2966), which McLendon describes as having primarily a pitch accent (tone); for Pne she explicitly says the accent is stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Northeastern Pomo (Pne) has a phonemic (contrastive, not phonologically predictable) STRESS accent, located mostly on the first or second syllable of the word; Halpern (ms.) suggests partial morphological predictability (accent on the root, as in Eastern Pomo verbs). Diachronically Pne 'to some extent' kept the proto accent contrast; deletion of pre-tonic *?/*h-initial syllables turned many proto second-syllable accents into initial accents. Also: 'Thus many proto forms which were accented on the second syllable, became Pn, Pc, Pe and Pne initially accented syllables.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing synchronic for Pne; a 'secondary accent' is used only in the reconstruction of two proto compounds (ASHES, TEARS), sec. 130, ts p. 37.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent 'mostly' on the first or second syllable (i.e. not exclusively); Pne preserved the phonemic accent only 'to some extent' (sec. 135), no further detail in the scanned range; per-language inventory charts (ts pp. 10-12 = pp. 26-28) mark 'stress' as a prosodic phoneme but the chart scanned is too poor to attribute columns; footnotes and Table 3 / lexicon (pp. 61-164) not scanned.
new_statements.identity_note: Northeastern Pomo = McLendon's 'Pne', one of the seven Pomoan daughter languages compared (data largely from Halpern's field material; the language had few or no speakers by the time of writing, cf. ts p. 8 'the material collected before the language ceased..'). The copy read is the 1971 typescript (CLA Oswalt.003.091) of McLendon 1973, quoted by typescript page and section number.

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing tension stands: Buckley 2020 (§3.6, draft p. 9) has Proto-Pomo stress on the root (second syllable of most words, initial when the root is monosyllabic) with Northeastern having often moved stress to the first syllable, while McLendon 1973 (pp. 33-34) says Northeastern Pomo 'to some extent' preserved the phonemic status of the proto accent, i.e. partly contrastive/lexical accent; the Moshinsky 1976 snippet adds that Northeastern suppresses stress on many morphemes and moves retained stress back onto the previously unstressed syllable. Golla 2011 could not be consulted on this.

Entry notes: under kʰáma 'Note the addition of -:- to the root moves stress to the second syllable from the left with the addition of the LOCATIVE/INSTRUMENTAL -wi'; under šá:ko 'Merriam's and Kroeber's records seem to indicate initial stress'.
